scenes.narration: Your program ran fine yesterday. Today Python can't find the package you know you installed.

Here's the real thing. One line of Python, one import, and a wall of red text. No module named requests. But you remember installing requests, so what happened? You're not imagining anything, and none of this is your fault.

uvStage.headline: The error [everybody] gets
uvStage.premise: A real terminal. One import, and the message every beginner has stared at.

steps.label: python -c "import requests"
steps.detail: installed. and Python cannot find it.

scenes.narration: Welcome along. By the end of this chapter you'll know exactly what breaks a working Python project, why nothing crashes when the breakage happens, and the shape of the thing that fixes all of it for good.

data.title: Why Python projects break
data.subtitle: uv, chapter zero · packages, versions, and one shelf

scenes.narration: And here's the one that really stings. Two projects on the same laptop. You install a package for the first project, you never once open the second, and the second project stops working. How? Hold that question, because the whole chapter is the answer.

uvStage.headline: You never [opened] the other one
uvStage.premise: Two folders on one laptop. Each is a project you wrote on a different week.

steps.label: cd report-tool && pip install "pygments==2.0.0"
steps.detail: you only touched this project

scenes.narration: To see why one project can break another, we need to look at what's actually sitting on your machine.

Picture a shelf. Every piece of code you install arrives as a sealed parcel, and the label on the parcel says two things: a name, and a version number. The name almost never changes, whereas the number changes constantly, and that number is where all the trouble starts.

uvStage.headline: A package is a [name and a number]
uvStage.premise: Picture a shelf. Each parcel is a package; the label says its name and version.

steps.label: pip download rich
steps.detail: one file. one name. one number.

steps.label: pip download rich==14.1.0
steps.detail: same name, different number, different file

stage.label: rich
stage.sub: the number is the part that moves

stage.label: rich
stage.sub: and the same shelf slot holds one of them

scenes.narration: Every parcel comes from the same place: one enormous public warehouse called PyPI, where anybody can put a parcel on the shelf and anybody can take one down. So when you type pip install, PyPI is where your machine goes looking.

uvStage.headline: They come from [one place]
uvStage.premise: One public warehouse. Anyone may add a parcel; your machine fetches one down.

steps.label: pip install rich
steps.detail: three hundred and ten kilobytes, off the stack

scenes.narration: Now watch what pip actually does. I asked for one parcel. Four arrived. Read the lines pip is printing out: markdown-it-py, pygments, mdurl. Nobody asked for those three. And look at the strange little bits of text beside each name, because those are the reasons. Rich can't run without pygments, so pip fetched pygments too.

uvStage.headline: One parcel, [four arrived]
uvStage.premise: Open a parcel and a note inside names the others the code cannot run without.

steps.label: pip install rich
steps.detail: the constraint beside each name is the reason

stage.label: rich
stage.sub: the one you actually asked for

uvStage.verdictSub: and mdurl was asked for by markdown-it-py

scenes.narration: Code that other code needs in order to run at all is called a dependency, and dependency is the single most important word in this whole course. Rich depends on pygments, which means pip must fetch pygments too. Markdown-it-py depends on mdurl, so mdurl arrives as well. That's two levels deep from one install, and nobody told you.

uvStage.headline: The word is [dependency]
uvStage.premise: Rich needs pygments. markdown-it-py needs mdurl. Two levels, from one command.

steps.label: pip show rich
steps.detail: rich says so itself

scenes.narration: Look at the order pip chose.

uvStage.headline: Read the [order]
uvStage.premise: Deepest first, and the parcel you actually asked for last of all.

steps.label: pip install rich
steps.detail: the floor first, then the thing standing on it

scenes.narration: So far everything works, which is exactly why the next part catches people out. Here's the bit nobody mentions.

There's only one shelf. Not one shelf per project — one shelf, for the entire machine. Your invoice app and your report tool are completely separate pieces of work, written months apart, and both of them reach into that same shelf for the same parcels.

uvStage.headline: Two projects, [one shelf]
uvStage.premise: One shelf for the whole machine. Every project on it reaches into the same one.

steps.label: pip list
steps.detail: one list, for everything you own

stage.label: pygments
stage.sub: the slot holds exactly one parcel

scenes.narration: And now the two projects want different things. Your invoice app was built against pygments two point twenty-one. Your report tool needs the old two point zero, because the report tool was written back when two point zero was current. Same parcel, two numbers, one slot, which means one of those projects is about to lose.

uvStage.headline: Same parcel, [two numbers]
uvStage.premise: The slot holds one parcel. Both projects need pygments, at versions that differ.

steps.label: pip install "pygments==2.0.0"
steps.detail: the report tool asks for the old parcel

stage.label: pygments
stage.sub: one slot, and one parcel fits in it

scenes.narration: So pip does the only thing pip can do, and narrates the whole business itself. Attempting uninstall. Found existing installation. Uninstalling. Successfully uninstalled. Pip lifted the parcel your invoice app depends on straight off the shelf, and pip never asked the invoice app what it thought.

uvStage.headline: The last install [wins]
uvStage.premise: The newcomer takes the slot. Whatever sat in the slot is carried away.

steps.label: pip install "pygments==2.0.0"
steps.detail: nobody asked the project that needed it

stage.label: pygments
stage.sub: and the newcomer takes the slot

scenes.narration: Then pip prints these two lines, one after the other. Pip says ERROR, and names the exact incompatibility pip has just created. And four lines later, in the same breath, pip says Successfully installed.

uvStage.headline: Pip said both of [these]
uvStage.premise: Two real lines, four lines apart, from one command. Read them together.

steps.label: pip install "pygments==2.0.0"
out: ERROR: pip’s dependency resolver does not currently take
into account all the packages that are installed.
steps.detail: broke rich, and reported success

scenes.narration: And then nothing happens. That's the part I want you to sit with. Run the code that's now broken and rich prints its text perfectly happily, because rich only reaches for the missing piece on certain code paths.

uvStage.headline: Nothing [crashes]
uvStage.premise: The environment is wrong. The program still runs. Both of those are true.

steps.label: python -c "from rich import print; print('hi')"
steps.detail: no crash. no warning. nothing at all.

steps.label: python -c "import rich; print(rich.__version__)"
steps.detail: still here, still broken underneath

scenes.narration: There's no red text, no traceback, no moment of discovery, which is exactly why the damage goes unnoticed. The shelf is simply wrong now, and the shelf stays wrong until some other line of code, on some other day, finally trips over the missing piece. That's why this costs people an entire afternoon: by the time the pain arrives, the command that caused the pain is long forgotten, and that command told you it succeeded.

uvStage.headline: Wrong now. Painful [later].
uvStage.premise: The break and the symptom are days apart, which is what makes it so expensive.

steps.label: git log --oneline -1
out: a1b3f90 tidy up the invoice totals
steps.detail: the real cause was three days earlier

stage.label: Tuesday
stage.sub: you installed something, and it said success

stage.label: Friday
stage.sub: a different project fails, for no visible reason

uvStage.verdictSub: which is why nobody connects the two

scenes.narration: One command would've told you, and almost nobody runs it. Pip check reads the shelf and says, in one plain sentence, which parcel is now wrong for which project.

uvStage.headline: The check [nobody] runs
uvStage.premise: One command reads the shelf and names the conflict in a plain sentence.

steps.label: pip check
steps.detail: pip knew. you just had to ask pip.

scenes.narration: And the loud error from the very beginning? Same shelf, different symptom. The requests parcel is real, requests exists, and you genuinely did install requests. Requests is just sitting on a different shelf from the one your program is standing at. So the loud error and the quiet one share a single cause: the shelf.

uvStage.headline: Real parcel, [wrong shelf]
uvStage.premise: The parcel exists and you installed it. Your program is standing somewhere else.

steps.label: python -c "import requests"
steps.detail: installed. just not on this shelf.

scenes.narration: So what would actually fix all of this? Before I answer, one quick check that the important word landed.

You asked for one package and four turned up. What do we call the three nobody asked for? Have a think, and pause the video here if you'd like a moment. Ready? They're dependencies — code your code needs in order to run.

quiz.question: You asked for one. Four arrived. The other three are called?
quiz.why: Code your code needs to run — fetched for you, noticed or not.

scenes.narration: Here's the answer, and honestly it's almost embarrassingly simple. Give every project a shelf of its own, and put a wall between the shelves so that nothing crosses over. Your invoice app keeps the new pygments, your report tool keeps the old pygments, and neither project can reach across and touch the other one's shelf.

uvStage.headline: A shelf [each]
uvStage.premise: One shelf per project, walled. Both versions exist, and neither reaches the other.

steps.label: ls invoice-app/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages
steps.detail: a folder. genuinely, that is all a shelf is.

stage.label: wall
stage.sub: neither project can reach the other shelf

uvStage.verdictSub: a folder of parcels owned by one project

scenes.narration: That folder of parcels, belonging to exactly one project, has a name: a virtual environment. So why does almost nobody keep one? Because of the ritual. You make the folder. You switch the folder on. You carry around in your head which folder you're currently in, because the terminal barely tells you. You switch the folder off when you leave. And the first time you forget any single one of those steps, you're straight back on the shared shelf without knowing.

uvStage.headline: The ritual nobody [keeps up]
uvStage.premise: Four steps, every project, every session. Miss one and you are back on the shared shelf.

steps.label: python -m venv .venv
steps.detail: step one, every single time

steps.label: source .venv/bin/activate
steps.detail: and now you must remember you are in it

scenes.narration: Unless something performs the ritual for you. There's a tool called uv, and removing that ritual is the entire reason uv exists. The folder gets made, used and forgotten on your behalf, every single time, and you never think about any of it. One command instead of four steps. We install uv in the next chapter.

uvStage.headline: One command, [instead]
uvStage.premise: The same four steps, performed for you, every time, without being asked.

steps.label: uv run main.py
steps.detail: made, used and forgotten, in one line

stage.label: uv run main.py
stage.sub: created, used and forgotten for you

scenes.narration: So, to recap. A package is a parcel with a name and a number, and asking for one parcel quietly brings others along. Your machine has one shelf, every project reaches into that shelf, and one slot holds exactly one version. And when two projects disagree, the last install wins, nothing crashes, and you find out weeks later.

points.text: A package is a name and a number
One shelf, and one slot per parcel
The last install wins, and says nothing
